description: RotaRovers olarak Mars'ı keşfedilebilir bir haritaya dönüştürüyoruz. Adımız "rota" ile "rover"dan geliyor: bilinmeyen bir yüzeyde doğru yolu bulmak. NASA verilerini katmanlı bir haritada birleştirip Mars'ta güvenli bir yürüyüşün planlanmasına yardım etmeyi amaçlıyoruz. İlgi alanlarımız Mars, gezegen bilimi ve insanlı keşif; becerilerimiz web geliştirme, veri analizi ve tasarım.
summary: RotaRovers Martian Map is a web-based tool that helps an astronaut plan a Marswalk and follow it on the surface. For a study area on the central mound of Gale crater (Mount Sharp), it computes a walking route from a NASA HiRISE terrain model, excludes all ground steeper than 20° (NASA's walking limit for lunar EVA suits, used here as a working value for Mars) and reaches five science stations selected for evidence of past water and habitability. The resulting 8.92 km round trip never exceeds 18.4° and stays within 1.74 km of the base, inside the walking radius of about 2 km that NASA plans for Artemis III. In planning mode, the map shows slope classes, the route, the scientific rationale and source for each station, and dated surface conditions from Curiosity and InSight, including an estimated radiation dose for the walk. In walking mode, it follows the astronaut and reports the current position, the next station, the remaining distance and time, and the turn-back point. The project addresses the two limits that decide whether a walk on foot is safe: terrain that a suited crew can walk and enough time to return to the base.
details:
RotaRovers Martian Map is a web-based planning and navigation tool for a crewed surface traverse (Marswalk) on Mars. It is built for a study area in Gale crater, on the crater's central mound (Mount Sharp), and supports the two phases of an extravehicular activity: planning the traverse before the crew leaves the base, and following it during the walk.

The traverse is derived from the HiRISE digital terrain model DTEEC_006855_1750_007501_1750_A01, produced from Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter stereo images. The elevation data are resampled to a 5 m grid and converted to slope. Cells steeper than 20° are treated as impassable; this threshold is the walking-slope limit given in NASA's Exploration EVA System Concept of Operations for lunar surface suits and is applied here as a working assumption for Mars. A least-cost path is then computed from the base through five science stations and back along the same path. The resulting round trip is 8.92 km long, with a maximum slope of 18.4° and 356 m of total ascent, and takes approximately 4 h 27 min at the planning rate of 2 km/h given in the same document. The farthest station lies 1.74 km from the base in a straight line, within the walking radius of approximately 2 km that NASA plans for Artemis III.

In planning mode, the map shows terrain shading, slope classes (15–20° as caution and above 20° as excluded terrain) and the route as separate layers. The five stations were selected by the team for evidence related to past water and habitability: a possible inverted channel, layered canyon walls, debris deposits attributed to water-assisted mass movement, sulfate-bearing strata, and a terrace at the northern end of the route. Each station is accompanied by a short scientific rationale and a published source. A conditions panel reports the most recent available Curiosity REMS weather observations, the nearest published wind record from InSight, and the average surface dose rate measured by Curiosity's RAD instrument, from which the dose for this traverse is estimated at about 0.12 mSv. All values are dated and presented as point measurements taken at other locations and times, not as forecasts.

In walking mode, the map follows the astronaut's position. The interface reports the current position and heading, the next station with its distance and estimated arrival time, the remaining distance and time to the base, and the turn-back point, defined as half of the total time budget. An elevation profile shows the gradient ahead, and a table lists the distance, duration, ascent and maximum slope of each leg. The traverse plan can be exported as a text EVA sheet. Since no positioning system is available on Mars, the astronaut's position is simulated with a slider and a playback function.

For a crew on foot, the two critical constraints are terrain that a suited astronaut can walk safely and the time and distance required to return to the base. The tool makes both constraints explicit before the traverse begins and keeps them visible throughout it.

The implementation is covered by 54 automated tests: 24 for the Python data pipeline and 30 for the web application. They verify that the maximum slope along the route remains below 20°, that the route is continuous and lies entirely within the terrain model, and that the route lengths computed by the pipeline and by the application agree when the Mars radius of 3,396.19 km is used.

The work has three main limitations. The 20° threshold is a lunar EVA value, as no equivalent value has been published for Mars. The environmental values were measured at other locations and times and do not describe the conditions at the study area on the day of a traverse. The astronaut's position during the walk is simulated rather than measured.

The data pipeline is written in Python using rasterio, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-image and pyproj. The application is built with React, TypeScript and Vite, uses OpenLayers with proj4 for a Mars equirectangular projection, and is hosted on Cloudflare Pages. The interface is available in English and Turkish, with light and dark themes.
